one_liner: Single-header C++11 flat_map/flat_set (sorted vector) plus small_vector and static_vector; claims to beat std::map for small sizes, unmeasured.
what_it_does: itlib is a collection of standalone single-header libraries; this entry covers four containers. itlib::flat_map and itlib::flat_set expose the std::map/std::set member functions over a sorted vector-like container chosen by the last template parameter (std::vector by default, itlib::static_vector or small_vector also work). itlib::small_vector is a std::vector with an inline buffer (16 elements by default) that spills to the heap, and itlib::static_vector is a fixed-capacity vector with no heap use.
how_it_is_fast: flat_map/flat_set are sorted-array maps: std::lower_bound binary search for lookups and contiguous storage for iteration, so there is no per-node allocation or pointer chasing, at the cost of O(n) element shifts on insert and erase. small_vector and static_vector avoid heap allocation while the size stays under the inline capacity; past that, small_vector grows by about 1.5x. There is no SIMD and no memcpy fast path: elements are moved one at a time through allocator_traits or placement new.
when_to_use: Small maps or sets (tens to low hundreds of entries) built once and then looked up or iterated many times, with keys that are cheap to compare and move
You want a std::map-shaped API without Boost: one MIT header, C++11, no dependencies
You need a fixed-capacity map with no heap use (embedded or real-time code): back flat_map with itlib::static_vector, as the unit tests do
Per-object short lists that usually stay under N elements (small_vector), or a known maximum size (static_vector)
when_not_to_use: Large maps with frequent inserts or erases in the middle: each one shifts O(n) elements, so the B-tree siblings fit better
Code that relies on std::map's stable iterators and references across insert and erase
Code that inserts or push_backs an element of the same small_vector or static_vector, or erases empty ranges of non-trivial types (see gotchas)
You need measured evidence of a speedup: the project publishes none; boost::container::flat_map has numbers, and a C++23 standard library that ships std::flat_map is the standard alternative
Bulk loading unsorted keys one insert at a time: there is no range insert, so this is O(n^2); build the vector and use the sorting constructor instead

integration.min_toolchain: C++11; CI builds with MSVC on Windows, GCC on Ubuntu and clang on macOS (compiler versions not stated); CMake 3.24 is needed only for the project's own build and tests
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the headers contain no internal locking
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: flat_map has std::map's lookup and modifier names, but its 4th template parameter is a container rather than an allocator, value_type is std::pair<Key, T> rather than pair<const Key, T>, insert and erase invalidate all iterators, and try_emplace, insert_or_assign, contains, extract, merge and range insert are missing

gotchas: Aliasing bug (found by code reading, not run): small_vector's push_back, emplace_back and insert call grow_at first, which moves the existing elements (into a new buffer when full, or shifting right in place) and destroys the sources (freeing an old heap buffer) before constructing from the argument. So v.push_back(v[0]) at capacity reads a destroyed or freed element, and v.insert(v.begin(), v[2]) copies whatever was shifted into slot 2 ({10,20,30,40} becomes {20,10,20,30,40}). static_vector::insert has the same in-place problem. std::vector guarantees both cases work, and the unit tests do not cover them.

Empty-range erase (code reading): erase(first, last) with first == last before end() runs shrink_at with num = 0, which destroys each element from first to end and then move-constructs it from itself. That is undefined behaviour for types such as std::string. The only empty-erase unit test uses int.

flat_map and flat_set iterators are the container's mutable iterators and flat_map's value_type has a non-const key, so writing through an iterator can silently break the sort order. The default comparator is a transparent operator< functor, not std::less<Key>. When duplicate keys are passed to the container or initializer_list constructor, std::sort (unstable) followed by std::unique decides which value survives, whereas std::map keeps the first.

small_vector's move constructor and move assignment are unconditionally noexcept but move a static-mode vector element by element, so a throwing T move calls std::terminate. Element transfers use std::move rather than move_if_noexcept, so there is no strong exception guarantee. With the default RevertToStaticBelow = 0 a vector that has spilled to the heap stays there even after clear(); a nonzero value makes erase, resize or pop_back move the elements back into the inline buffer, invalidating all iterators.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over boost::container::flat_map/flat_set (the closest sibling, and the one with numbers: about 1.1-2.5x faster than std::set at sizes 2-128) only when you cannot take a Boost dependency or want to swap the backing container, for example to static_vector. For large maps, tlx btree_map, cpp-btree, frozenca/BTree or fast-containers are the measured choices.
verified_claims_summary: Nothing has been measured. The only performance statement is the header comment that flat_map and flat_set 'generally perform much faster than std::map [std::set] for smaller sets of elements', with no sizes, compiler or hardware. The repo's only benchmark target (test/b-rand_dist.cpp, built with picobench) covers random distributions, and a web search found no third-party numbers.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-10-06, 451 commits, 212 stars, CI with sanitizers on MSVC, GCC and clang), MIT-licensed and easy to vendor one header at a time, but tier D: no performance numbers exist, and code reading shows that small_vector and static_vector mishandle self-referencing insert and push_back and empty-range erase of non-trivial types.
